title: AIDLC project configuration
description: Per-project configuration for the Bee-Logical Claude AIDLC framework. Lives at the workspace control plane in .claude/aidlc.config.json. Supports a single repo (mono, the default) or many repos (poly).

configVersion.description: Contract version of THIS file, bumped only when a key changes meaning or is removed (additive keys do not bump it, which is why every object here allows additional properties). Written by /aidlc:init and /aidlc:adopt-apply so a later plugin version can tell an old config from a current one and upgrade it in place. Absent means the file predates the stamp: it is then classified by SHAPE — a flat pipeline.gates with no `verify`, no adoption block, no configVersion — because a version stamp cannot be applied retroactively to files already in the wild. Nothing reads this to decide behaviour; it exists so an upgrade is a deliberate, shown diff rather than a guess about which keys a reader may trust.

aidlcVersion.description: The aidlc plugin version that last wrote this file, e.g. '0.33.0'. Diagnostic, and the input to upgrade detection: a config written by an older plugin may lack blocks the current one reads, and saying which version wrote it turns 'why is this key missing' into one lookup.

key.description: Uppercase work-item ID prefix, e.g. PROJ.

workspace.description: Workspace topology. Absent or layout=mono → single repo (the top-level git/stack/ux blocks apply). layout=poly → the repos[] array defines each git repo; this file sits at the workspace control plane. The product repos are USUALLY subfolders of the control plane, but need not be: in a multi-root IDE workspace (a *.code-workspace folders[] list) the roots may live under different parents or on different drives, and a repo entry then carries an absolute path. The control plane is the folder holding the .code-workspace file when there is one, else the opened folder — never a product repo.

root.description: Base directory for RELATIVE repo paths, itself relative to this config's location. Usually '.'. May be omitted entirely — it is only a base for resolution, not an assertion that the repos are nested; a repos[] entry with an absolute path does not consult it.

crossRepoSplit.description: Poly only. The work-item tier at which cross-repo work is split into single-repo RUNNABLE units (one run = one repo = one branch = one PR — that leaf is always single-repo either way). 'story' (default, recommended): a Feature fans out to per-repo Stories; each Story is one repo and its Tasks are that repo's breakdown. Fits ADO's Epic→Feature→Story→Task hierarchy natively and makes one Story = one PR. 'task': a User Story is a cross-repo UMBRELLA that captures one unit of user value, and its child Tasks are the per-repo runnable units (API task → backend repo, UI task → frontend repo, migration task → db repo); the Story rolls up when its tasks complete. Both are supported; pick the one your ADO board is authored for. See aidlc:work-items → Cross-repo split tier.

architecture.description: The project's shape as DERIVED FROM REQUIREMENTS by /aidlc:bootstrap, rather than answered up front. init may write {status:pending} to defer topology/stack/repos to bootstrap (the greenfield-from-requirements flow); bootstrap then infers them, sets status=resolved, and writes workspace.layout + (stack or repos[]) + workspace.crossRepoSplit to match. A human who authored those fields directly can leave this absent (treated as resolved).

status.description: pending = init deferred the architecture; the topology/stack/repos in this file are placeholders and /aidlc:bootstrap will overwrite them from the requirements. resolved = the architecture has been determined (by bootstrap or a human) and workspace.layout/stack/repos are authoritative. Absent ⇒ resolved.

style.description: Architecture style bootstrap inferred from the requirements, biased to the SIMPLEST that fits (YAGNI). Drives the mono/poly + repos[] shape and crossRepoSplit: monolith / modular-monolith ⇒ mono (single repo, modules internal); microservices ⇒ poly (service-per-repo). Recorded for traceability.

resolvedBy.description: What set the architecture: "/aidlc:bootstrap" (inferred from a requirements document), "codebase-scan" (derived from existing code by /aidlc:adopt and applied by /aidlc:adopt-apply — see the adoption block for the provenance), "init", or "human".

rationale.description: One-line why, grounded in the requirements (the split/no-split signal bootstrap acted on).

adoption.description: Provenance for configuration DERIVED FROM AN EXISTING CODEBASE. Written by /aidlc:adopt-apply when it applies an approved profile; absent on a greenfield project. It is what makes adoption idempotent and drift detectable: re-running against the same commit must propose no changes, and a later scan compares itself against these values rather than rewriting the file. Never hand-edit it — it describes what a scan actually saw.

scannedAt.description: UTC ISO-8601 timestamp of the scan this configuration came from (profile.scan.scannedAt).

commit.description: The commit the scan ran against. A re-scan at the same commit proposes nothing; at a different commit, the diff is the project's drift, not a rewrite.

profileVersion.description: Contract version of the profile that was applied. A consumer that does not recognise it must say so and stop rather than read the file optimistically.

profilePath.description: Where the profile this was applied from lives, relative to the control plane.

depth.description: How deep the originating scan looked. A shallower scan leaves more facts unknown, so a quick-scan-derived config is expected to carry gaps — recorded here so nobody mistakes them for findings.

appliedAt.description: When the profile was applied to this file, which may be later than the scan.

unmanaged.description: Surfaces deliberately left OUT of AIDLC's management (a repo or package the team is not piloting on). Named here so a later scan does not keep proposing them and a reader can tell 'not adopted' from 'missed'.

only.description: The surfaces a PARTIAL adoption was scoped to (`/aidlc:adopt-apply --only <repo|package>`), recorded positively rather than only as the inverse. A pilot on one repo of six leaves five roots that are neither configured nor listed as excluded, and without this a later reader cannot tell a deliberate pilot from an adoption that fell over halfway. Absent means the whole workspace was in scope.

upgrades.description: One entry per in-place upgrade of this file by a newer plugin version. Recorded because an upgrade rewrites configuration a team depends on: the diff was shown and approved at the time, and this is what lets somebody six months later see WHICH keys were moved and by what. Never hand-authored.

from.description: The plugin version (or 'unstamped' where the file carried no aidlcVersion and was classified by shape).

to.description: The plugin version that performed the upgrade.

changes.description: One line per key added, moved or renamed, e.g. 'pipeline.gates.{steps,repos} → pipeline.gates.verify.{steps,repos}'. A value a human authored is never rewritten by an upgrade — only relocated, and only with the move shown.

seeded.description: What a previous /aidlc:adopt-apply CONTRIBUTED to each union-merged array. Not the array itself — the record of our own contributions, which is what makes the union three-way. Without it, a seed missing from the array is indistinguishable from a seed the team deliberately REMOVED, so every re-apply silently restores the deletion; adopt §9 names 'a deliberately narrowed securityReviewPaths' as exactly the human edit that must never be reverted. A withheld seed stays listed here — it is the record of 'we offered this and the team said no'. Resolved by skills/adopt-apply/seed-paths.mjs.

securityReviewPaths.description: The securityReviewPaths entries adoption has ever contributed. A path here but absent from pipeline.securityReviewPaths was removed on purpose and must not be re-added.

writes.description: What adoption actually wrote, per file — the manifest that makes clean removal possible. Without it, removing AIDLC means guessing which lines in CLAUDE.md and settings.json were the team's and which were ours, and the safe guess (delete the file) destroys the team's own content. Written by /aidlc:adopt-apply for every file it touched; /aidlc:remove reads it and asks about anything not listed.

ownership.description: created: the file did not exist and adoption made it — removal may delete it outright. merged: the file was the project's and adoption added sections or keys to it — removal reverts THOSE sections and nothing else. rendered: an AIDLC-owned file generated from config (rules/git-workflow.md) — removal deletes it, but a human may have edited it since, so removal shows the diff against what was rendered before deleting.

sections.description: For ownership=merged, the specific sections or keys that were added — 'CLAUDE.md ## Commands', 'permissions.allow[+12 entries]'. This is the whole value of the manifest: it is the difference between reverting our edit and reverting the file.

adrs.description: Retroactive ADRs written by /aidlc:adopt-adr, one entry per decision. This is the de-duplication key for re-adoption: a later scan proposes an ADR only for a decisionKind that does not appear here, so re-running never offers a second ADR for a decision already recorded. It also lets a reader see which of the code's embedded decisions have been written down and which are still undocumented.

decisionKind.description: The profile's adrCandidates[].decisionKind — framework, data-store, auth-model, tenancy-model, api-style, deployment-topology, messaging, migration-strategy, frontend-architecture, build-tooling, observability, other.

adr.description: Path of the written ADR, e.g. docs/adr/0007-shared-schema-tenancy.md — or the URL of a pre-existing external doc that already records the decision (then nothing was written; it is linked from the index).

repo.description: The repo whose code evidences the decision; omit for a workspace-wide one.

rationaleConfirmed.description: False means the ADR still says *rationale not recorded — confirm with the team*. It stays false until a human fills it in: the scan never sets it true, because it never knew the why.

repos.description: Declared git repos. Empty (or omitted) means mono — a single repo synthesized from the top-level git/stack/ux blocks. Non-empty means poly. When architecture.status=pending these are placeholders until /aidlc:bootstrap resolves them.

name.description: Short unique id used to route items and label PRs, e.g. backend.

path.description: Repo checkout path: either relative to workspace.root, or an ABSOLUTE path. A repo need not live under the control plane — a multi-root IDE workspace can place it under a different parent, on another drive, or on a UNC share. Absolute is the correct spelling in those cases; a relative path that escapes the control plane (../foo) is legal but harder to read. When a repo is NOT nested under the control plane, the control plane's .gitignore/gitlink protection is inapplicable to it (there is no shared git index to stage it into) and every consumer must quote the path — it may contain spaces.

role.description: Free-text description used as a routing hint by the orchestrator.

adoptedFromRoot.description: The adoption profile's workspace.roots[].name this entry was built from, when it DIFFERS from `name`. Profile root names come from the .code-workspace `name` override (adopt §1 honours it), while `name` here is the short routing id — two namespaces, so `billing-api` in the profile can be `api` here. /aidlc:adopt-adr and /aidlc:adopt-backlog resolve a finding's or candidate's `root` through this field; without it an adoption-born item is stamped with a repo name that matches no entry, resolve-gate returns an EMPTY step list, and the item verifies against nothing and reports green.

mode.description: remote (default): push the branch and open a PR; a human merges it. local: no remote — after green verify the pipeline integrates via a confirmed local --no-ff merge into the default branch.

labels.description: Label hints: an item labeled with any of these routes to this repo.

ux.description: Per-repo UX config for frontend repos (overrides the top-level ux block for this repo).

default.description: The fallback repo when routing is otherwise ambiguous. At most one repo should set this.

packages.description: Mono-mode package registry — one git repo holding many independently-owned packages (pnpm/npm/yarn workspaces, Nx, Turborepo, Lerna, a Maven multi-module build, a Cargo workspace). In poly, each repos[] entry carries its own packages[] instead. This is deliberately NOT a third workspace.layout value: the git boundary is what repos[] means, and a monorepo has one, so it stays layout=mono (or one poly repo entry) with the package dimension expressed here. That is also what makes the hybrid workspace representable — a monorepo root beside single-app repos, without a new layout.

saas.description: Mono-mode SaaS runtime constraints. In poly, each repo carries its own saas block.

git.description: Mono-mode single-repo git settings. Ignored when repos[] is non-empty (poly).

mode.description: remote (default): push the branch and open a PR; a human merges it. local: no remote — after green verify the pipeline integrates via a confirmed local --no-ff merge into the default branch.

stack.description: Mono-mode stack. In poly, each repo carries its own stack.

ceremony.description:
The FLOOR for how much process a change gets (aidlc:ceremony). It only ever raises the tier, never lowers it — the pipeline still escalates above the floor when the work or a risk trigger warrants.

"direct" (default): a small, obvious, low-consequence change is edited, gated and committed on the current branch with no work item, no run file and no PR. Work that warrants a trail still gets one. This is the setting that makes the tool usable for a typo, and the reason it exists: charging a one-line fix the same process tax as a story does not make the story safer, it makes people stop using the pipeline for the changes that genuinely needed it.

"tracked": every change gets at least a branch and a run file — nothing is ever untracked — but items and PRs remain optional. A middle ground for a small team that wants a trail without a ticket per edit.

"full": every change goes through the whole pipeline (work item, requirements, verification cadence, PR). A legitimate choice for a regulated or audit-bound team, and what AIDLC did unconditionally before 0.36.0.

Independent of the floor, five escalation triggers pull a change UP regardless of this setting and regardless of the user's preference, because each names something not recoverable by noticing it later: auth/tenant-isolation paths, a destructive migration under expand-contract, a declared apiContracts path, code an in-flight run already owns, and an explicit pipeline request. None fire on an absent config field.

securityReviewPaths.description: Path globs whose modification makes a diff security-relevant — read by the run skill's risk-based security cadence. /aidlc:adopt-apply SEEDS this from the scan's saas.securityReviewPathSeeds (tenant isolation, auth, billing, compliance-governed paths) by UNION, never replacement: a path a human added stays, and a seeded path is added beside it. Two entry classes are not merely cadence inputs — a diff touching a tenant-isolation or auth path triggers security review regardless of the configured cadence (see saas.tenantIsolationPaths / saas.authPaths), because 'we only review per-epic' is not an acceptable answer for a cross-tenant data leak.

envFileAccess.description: Whether the pipeline may read or change env files (.env, .env.example, .env.local, …). "deny" (default): the hooks hard-block every read/edit/write of an env file — they can carry secrets, and non-secret variable names/shape are meant to live in a human-maintained .env.example. "ask": the pipeline may touch env files, but EVERY read/change is surfaced to the user to approve or reject (the confirmation prompt shows the exact diff/content), keeping the human in the loop. Enforced by two hooks so no tool path escapes it: env-guard.mjs governs the Read/Edit/Write tools, and guard.mjs mirrors it on the Bash path (> .env redirects, tee/cp/sed -i writes, cat .env reads). Both resolve the switch by walking up from the env file's own location to the nearest aidlc.config.json, so one control-plane setting governs every repo's env files in a poly workspace regardless of the session cwd. Both fail closed (no config found up the tree, or a malformed one ⇒ "deny"). This is a hook-based switch, not a static Read(.env*) deny, because a static deny can never be relaxed; settings.json carries these paths in its "ask" list only, as a fail-safe floor for when the hooks are not running. Opting in is a single edit here — no settings.json change needed.

implementFanout.description:
Whether ONE work item's plan may be implemented by several agents concurrently, when its plan tasks touch provably disjoint paths (aidlc:run §6; reference implementation skills/run/resolve-fanout.mjs, semantics pinned by resolve-fanout.test.mjs). Absent ⇒ enabled with the defaults below, so no existing config needs migrating.

Why this is safe, and what it is NOT. Architecture D7 serializes anything that mutates a shared tree, and for one item that has always meant a single implementer. The rule stands; the reading was too broad. Six screens getting the same treatment touch six disjoint FILES — the shared thing is git, not the code. So the fan-out removes the racing committer instead of the parallelism: the agents edit and report, and the ORCHESTRATOR commits each task's declared paths in plan order. One writer to git, always. This is a wall-clock optimization with no quality trade-off — it does not reduce review, and the resolved gate still runs (once, after the window lands).

What the resolver refuses to guess, because each failure is silent: a task with no declared `paths` is never parallelized; two globs that cannot be cheaply compared are assumed to overlap; and disjoint paths do NOT imply independence — a task whose output a later task imports must say so via the plan's `foundation`/`dependsOn`, since no path analysis can see an import edge. Over-serializing costs wall-clock and says so; under-serializing loses code and says nothing.

enabled.description: false ⇒ every item is implemented by a single agent start to finish (pre-0.35.0 behaviour). The resolver still runs and still reports, it just holds every task serial with that reason stated.

maxAgents.description: Most concurrent implementers in one window. Hard-capped at 5 (values above are clamped, not rejected), mirroring /aidlc:sprint's cap: one work item must not be able to spawn a fleet. There is nothing to gain above the number of genuinely disjoint tasks a plan produces.

minGroup.description: Smallest window worth dispatching in parallel. Floored at 2 — a 'parallel' batch of one is just a serial step with extra bookkeeping. Raise it to 3+ to only fan out when the win is clearly worth the dispatch overhead.

sharedPaths.description:
Extra paths that must always have exactly one writer, ADDED to (never replacing) the built-in list: dependency manifests and lockfiles, barrel/aggregator modules (index.ts, __init__.py, mod.rs), route tables, i18n catalogs, global styles, tool config, test snapshots, migrations, and every path named in saas.apiContracts. A task touching any of these is held serial with the matching pattern stated as its reason.

This is the one setting a stranger to the codebase cannot infer: a project's OWN aggregator — a central theme file, a generated registry, a hand-maintained DI container — belongs here. The built-in list catches the conventional ones only.

gates.description: The things that gate a pipeline run's progression. `ambiguousRequirements` gates progression when a requirement is unclear; `verify` gates it on quality. They are separate concerns that happen to share this block — do not conflate them.

ambiguousRequirements.description: What the pipeline does when a requirement is ambiguous at the requirements phase. assume-and-log (default): take the most reasonable reading, log it as an assumption on the run file and the item, keep going. ask-human: stop and ask. Read by aidlc:run at the requirements gate.

verify.description:
The project's REAL verification gate, replacing the assumption that every repo runs npm scripts. An ordered list of steps the run skill executes top to bottom in the verify phase; a repo with no package.json completes a full run on its own gate (ruff + pytest, mvn -B verify, cargo test) because the gate came from the project rather than from AIDLC. Populated by /aidlc:adopt-apply from a scan, or written by hand. Absent ⇒ the run falls back to the CLAUDE.md Commands block.

RESOLUTION LAYERS, IT DOES NOT REPLACE. Walk from the NARROWEST applicable list to the broadest — repos.<repo>.packages.<pkg>.steps, then packages.<pkg>.steps (the mono package layer), then repos.<repo>.steps, then the top-level steps. Each layer contributes its steps in its own declared order, but only for gate names no narrower layer already claimed. So the narrowest layer that mentions a gate owns both its definition and its position, and broader layers top up the gates nobody narrower mentioned.

This buys two properties, both of which the obvious 'take the narrowest list' reading gets wrong: a package that declares its own `test` still inherits the repo's `lint` (taking only the narrowest list silently loses it, and a gate that vanished is indistinguishable from one that passed — the same class of failure as deleting an `absent` entry), and a repo that declares [test, lint] runs test first, because its ordering is a deliberate statement that a broader default's ordering must not override. To make a package genuinely skip a repo-level gate, declare that gate at the package level with `status: "absent"` — an explicit, self-documenting opt-out that still shows up in the run's coverage-hole report. The reference implementation is `skills/run/resolve-gate.mjs` (with `resolve-gate.test.mjs` pinning the semantics).

maxItemMinutes.description: The per-item budget for the whole gate. A step whose scope is repo and whose known duration exceeds this is scoped down per item (affected set, or a changed-paths subset) with the full suite left to CI — and the run file records WHICH subset ran, so a green run is never mistaken for a full-suite green.

steps.description: The default/mono gate. In poly this is the fallback for a repo that declares none.

packages.description: Mono-mode per-package overrides, keyed by packages[].name — the layer a monorepo needs when there is no repos[] entry to hang them off. Narrower than `steps`, broader than a poly repo's own packages block. In poly, use repos.<repo>.packages instead.
Per-package overrides inside a monorepo, keyed by package name. This is the dimension a monorepo needs: one git repo, many packages with their own gates and cadence.

verification.description: Per-agent verification cadence — the pipeline's biggest recurring cost. Each agent runs on its own schedule so tokens are spent only where they earn it. Defaults are economical: reviewer/qa on-demand, security per-epic (confirmed). The deterministic CI gate (lint/format/typecheck/boundaries/tests) runs regardless and is the per-item floor.

mode.description: auto: agent cadences decide. manual: skip all agents, human reviews the PR. ask: prompt per item.

reviewer.description: Adversarial diff review vs AC + coding standards.

qa.description: Full suite + missing-test authoring. (Bug repro-first still runs at implement.)

security.description: Deep security pass. risk-based = per-item only when the diff is risky.

securityConfirm.description: Ask the user to confirm before running the security pass.

ux.description: Mono-mode / default UX config. In poly, each frontend repo may carry its own ux block.

pluginFeedback.description: Plugin self-feedback (dogfood) channel. When enabled, the pipeline records AIDLC-plugin friction it hits during a run — gaps, wrong/missing guidance, steps it had to work around, skill/agent/template bugs (distinct from project bugs) — as structured entries in a local inbox, for the plugin maintainer to triage. Default off, so normal projects stay quiet; a project used to dogfood the plugin turns it on. See the aidlc:dogfood skill.

enabled.description: Turn on plugin self-feedback capture for this workspace.

inbox.description: Path (relative to the control plane) of the append-only feedback inbox the pipeline writes to.

packages.description: Packages inside ONE git repo — the dimension a monorepo needs and repos[] cannot express, because repos[] means a git boundary and a monorepo has exactly one. Each entry routes work exactly as a repo entry does (labels, role, an optional single default), and the runnable leaf is unchanged: one item = one branch = one PR, now scoped to a package. Per-package gates live at pipeline.gates.verify.packages.<name>.steps (mono) or pipeline.gates.verify.repos.<repo>.packages.<name>.steps (poly), and resolve by LAYERING over the repo's — a package that declares its own test still inherits the repo's lint.

name.description: The package's own name as its manifest declares it (`@acme/web`, `acme-worker`, a Maven artifactId). It keys the per-package gate overrides and labels the PR, so it must be what the project calls it — never a folder name invented at adoption.

path.description: Path to the package, relative to its repo root (not to the control plane).

role.description: Free-text routing hint, same contract as a repo's role.

labels.description: Label hints: an item labeled with any of these routes to this package.

stack.description: Per-package stack, overriding the repo's for this package. A Next.js app beside a Python worker in one repo is the normal case, and resolving stack per repo would hand the worker the web standards.

ux.description: Per-package UX config for a frontend package, overriding the repo's ux block — the design pod runs against this package's dev server, not the repo's.

dependsOn.description: Sibling package names this one depends on, from the manifests. Cross-package work sequences on this exactly as cross-repo work sequences on item dependsOn: a change to a shared package lands before its consumers. The graph must be acyclic.

releasable.description: True when the repo's tooling versions and publishes this package on its own cadence (changesets, independent Lerna versioning, nx release). False or absent means it releases with the repo — /aidlc:release must then say so plainly instead of cutting a per-package release the tooling does not support.

default.description: The fallback package when routing within this repo is otherwise ambiguous. At most one package per repo should set this.

saas.description:
The runtime constraints that change how code must be WRITTEN — not what the stack is, but what a safe change to it looks like. Derived by /aidlc:adopt from static evidence and applied on approval; fed to the implementer, reviewer and security agents as hard constraints on every item that touches the paths named here. Everything is OPTIONAL and an absent field means no constraint was evidenced, which is different from 'no constraint exists' — the briefs then stay silent rather than asserting one.

This block informs and triggers review; it does not gate merges by itself. The two exceptions are deliberate and both conditional on evidenced facts: a destructive migration where liveDataConstraint is expand-contract is a review BLOCKER, and a diff touching an apiContracts path or a tenantIsolationPaths/authPaths entry gets reviewed regardless of the configured cadence.

tenancy.description: How tenants are isolated. shared-schema is the most constraining: every query must filter by the tenant key, and a missing filter is a cross-tenant data leak rather than a bug. Omit it entirely when the scan could not evidence it — a guess here misdirects every review.

tenantKey.description: The column/claim that carries tenancy in a shared-schema model, e.g. tenant_id or org_id. Named so a reviewer can check a new query against it.

tenantIsolationPaths.description: Paths implementing the isolation mechanism (scoping middleware, row-level-security policies, the per-tenant connection resolver). A diff here is security-reviewed regardless of cadence.

authPaths.description: Paths implementing authentication, authorization, SSO, RBAC or sessions. Security-reviewed regardless of cadence.

billingPaths.description: Paths implementing billing, subscription, entitlement or metering logic — revenue-critical, so they join securityReviewPaths.

featureFlags.description: The flag system in use, when flags are how this project releases. When present, the implementer brief states that user-visible changes ship behind a flag — merging is then not the same event as shipping.

required.description: True when the project's convention is that every user-visible change ships behind a flag. The implementer is briefed accordingly; a change that cannot be flagged is then something to raise, not to route around.

migrations.description: The migration tool and where its migrations live.

tool.description: Prisma, TypeORM, Alembic, Flyway, Liquibase, EF Core, Rails, Django, golang-migrate.

liveDataConstraint.description: expand-contract: schema changes run against live data (shared by tenants), so they must add → migrate → backfill → remove across releases, and a DESTRUCTIVE migration in one step — a dropped or renamed column, a narrowed type, a NOT NULL added to an existing column — is a review BLOCKER rather than a style note. not-required only where the evidence supports it (a single-tenant install migrated on upgrade, a pre-launch schema).

apiContracts.description: Public/consumer contracts. A diff touching one of these paths marks the item CONTRACT-AFFECTING, which triggers breaking-change review regardless of the configured cadence — the whole point of recording them.

public.description: True when external consumers depend on it, so a break is a customer-visible incident rather than an internal refactor.

environments.description: Environments this project deploys to, from CI/CD config.

freezeWindows.description: Declared change freezes or release trains. Surfaced at integration when a merge would violate one — the pipeline reports it and asks; it never merges through a freeze silently, and never blocks on an unevidenced one.

when.description: In the project's own terms, e.g. 'Fri 16:00 → Mon 09:00 UTC' or 'the last week of each quarter'.

source.description: Where it is declared — the CI schedule guard, the documented calendar. An unsourced freeze is a rumour.

compliance.description: Compliance regimes governing change here, each with the SIGNAL that evidenced it. This raises the review cost of every future change, so an inferred regime is an expensive wrong answer — the signal is what makes it auditable.

signal.description: What evidenced it, e.g. 'BAA referenced in docs/security/hipaa.md:12', 'PCI SAQ-A in compliance/'. Never 'the README says the product is secure'.

messaging.description: Queues, brokers, streams, schedulers and webhooks. Their message shapes are contracts with consumers that no contract file records, so a changed shape is a breaking change a diff review can miss.

observability.description: Error tracking / metrics / tracing in use. Recorded because production incidents are a legitimate intake source, and because a diff that drops instrumentation is a regression tests do not catch.

source.description: Where this block came from. `codebase-scan`: derived by /aidlc:adopt with evidence in the adoption profile. `human`: someone authored it, and a later scan must surface a disagreement as a choice rather than overwriting it — the same contract as gitConventions.conventionsSource.

gateSteps.description: An ORDERED gate sequence. Order is the contract — the run skill executes it top to bottom and stops at the first required failure.

name.description: Short stable id — lint, typecheck, test, format, build, boundaries, or a project-specific one. Unique within its step list.

status.description: present: the project has this gate and `cmd` runs it. absent: the project provably does NOT have it — kept in the list on purpose so the run reports it in `## Findings` as a coverage hole. not-applicable: the STACK has no such step (a Django service is deployed from source so has no build; Go type-checks during `go build` so has no separate typecheck) — carried through so the run can list it as inapplicable, and never reported as a coverage hole, because a finding nobody can ever close teaches the team to skip the section. Neither absent nor not-applicable carries a cmd, neither is ever `required`, and neither is counted green. Deleting the entry instead of recording it is what makes a missing gate invisible. This enum must stay identical to the adoption profile's `definitions.gate.properties.status`, which /aidlc:adopt-apply copies values through from.

cmd.description: The command verbatim, as the project runs it (`pnpm test`, `uv run pytest`, `mvn -B verify`, `cargo clippy -- -D warnings`). Required when status=present.

cwd.description: Directory to run it from, relative to the repo root. Omit for the repo root itself.

required.description: Whether a failure blocks the item. false = advisory, reported but non-blocking.

scope.description: What it runs over per item. affected: an affected-graph runner's affected set (Nx/Turbo) — the cheap correct choice where one exists, and the run report must name the affected set. changed-paths: a diff-derived subset, for a suite too slow to run whole.

timeoutMinutes.description: Hard cap for this step. Exceeding it is a gate failure with a distinct diagnosis (hung/slow), not a code failure.

environmentDependent.description: True when the step needs services (Docker Compose, testcontainers, a live DB, a broker). A failure is then diagnosed as **environment unavailable** rather than **code broken** — the distinction that stops a run report from blaming the diff for a missing database.

providedByHook.description: A pre-existing hook manager (husky, pre-commit, lefthook) already runs this at commit time. The AIDLC pre-commit layer must not duplicate it.

gitConventions.description: The project's OWN git and review conventions, adopted rather than imposed. These apply to a mono repo's top-level git block and to each repos[] entry alike. Where a project has no convention of its own, AIDLC's defaults apply and conventionsSource records that they are defaults — a default presented as a detected fact is the failure these fields exist to prevent.

integrationBranch.description: The branch feature work branches FROM and integrates INTO, when that is not `defaultBranch` — GitFlow's `develop`. Load-bearing: with this set, the pipeline must not branch from or open PRs against `main`. Omit it when the project integrates into its default branch (setting it equal to defaultBranch is a configuration error, not a no-op).

commitStyle.description: The commit-message convention actually in use. `conventional` = feat|fix|chore(scope): …; `id-prefixed` = e.g. `JIRA-123 …`; `mixed` = the history has no single convention, in which case the pipeline follows the project's dominant form without enforcing one.

mergeStrategy.description: How the project integrates a branch. The integration step honours it — a squash-only repo must not receive a --no-ff merge commit.

longLivedBranches.description: Branches/patterns that must never be deleted or force-updated (`develop`, `release/*`, `hotfix/*`). Distinguishes a permanent branch from a stale feature branch.

hotfixRoute.description: The project's distinct path for production incidents, in one line, where it has one — so an urgent item is not forced through the normal flow.

contribution.description: `direct`: push branches to this remote. `fork`: the user cannot push here, so the integration path is push to a fork and open a PR against the upstream. Detected at adoption time precisely so a run does not fail at its first push.

upstreamRemote.description: Name of the upstream remote when contribution is `fork` (conventionally `upstream`). The PR targets this repo, not the fork.

conventionsSource.description: Where the conventions in this block came from. `codebase-scan`: derived from this project's history/host settings with evidence in the adoption profile. `default`: the project had none and AIDLC's defaults were used — say so rather than implying detection. `human`: someone authored them, and a scan must never silently overwrite them.
